```{r}
fmt_tbl <- function(df, right = NULL) {
  df <- dplyr::mutate(df, dplyr::across(dplyr::any_of("Year"), as.integer))
  right <- union(names(df)[vapply(df, is.numeric, TRUE)], right)
  flextable::flextable(df) |>
    flextable::fontsize(size = 9, part = "all") |>
    flextable::align(align = "center", part = "header") |>
    flextable::align(j = setdiff(names(df), right), align = "left", part = "body") |>
    flextable::align(j = right, align = "right", part = "body") |>

    flextable::padding(padding.top = 1, padding.bottom = 1, part = "all") |>
    flextable::set_table_properties(layout = "autofit", width = 1)
}
```

```{r}
trees_uncertainty <- function(ci_half_width) 0.524417 / 1.645006 * ci_half_width

buffer_table <- c(none = 0.25, `1` = 0.20, `2` = 0.15, `3` = 0.20,
                  `1,2` = 0.10, `1,3` = 0.15, `2,3` = 0.10, `1,2,3` = 0.05)

trees_buffer <- function(mitigating = "none", after_reversal = FALSE) {
  buffer_table[[mitigating]] + if (after_reversal) 0.05 else 0
}

kept <- function(ci_half_width, mitigating = "none", after_reversal = FALSE) {
  1 - trees_uncertainty(ci_half_width) - trees_buffer(mitigating, after_reversal)
}

break_even <- function(...) (1 - trees_buffer(...)) / (0.524417 / 1.645006)

crediting_level <- function(x, years) sum(x[years]) / 5

accounts <- national |>
  dplyr::filter(year >= 2012) |>
  dplyr::mutate(reference = year <= 2016)

level_whole  <- sum(accounts$net[accounts$reference]) / 5

credits <- accounts |>

split_pos <- credits[["Disaggregated reductions (Mt)"]] > 0
whole_pos <- credits[["Undisaggregated reductions (Mt)"]] > 0

classify <- function(n) {
  base <- forest_co2[forest_co2$year < min(forest_co2$year) + n, ]
  thr <- mean(base$co2) + 2 * stats::sd(base$co2)
  data.frame(`Baseline (years)` = n,
             Period = if (nrow(base) < n) NA_character_ else
               paste(min(base$year), max(base$year), sep = "-"),
             `Threshold (kt)` = if (nrow(base) < n) NA_real_ else round(thr),
             `Years classified natural` = if (nrow(base) < n) "baseline longer than the series" else
               paste(forest_co2$year[forest_co2$co2 > thr], collapse = ", "),
             check.names = FALSE)
}
baselines <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c(13, 20, 30), classify))

# Australia's rule on Canada's two lines: the natural disturbance line is left out only in a year whose
# forest fire emissions exceed the mean of the 13-year baseline, Australia's length, by two standard deviations
years13 <- forest_co2$year[forest_co2$year < min(forest_co2$year) + 13]
first13 <- forest_co2$co2[forest_co2$year %in% years13]
natural_years <- forest_co2$year[forest_co2$co2 > mean(first13) + 2 * stats::sd(first13)]
accounts <- dplyr::mutate(accounts, rule = dplyr::if_else(year %in% natural_years, human, net))
level_rule <- sum(accounts$rule[accounts$reference]) / 5
credits <- credits |>
  dplyr::mutate(`Australian rule emissions (Mt)` = accounts$rule[!accounts$reference],
                `Australian rule reductions (Mt)` = round(level_rule - `Australian rule emissions (Mt)`, 1))
rule_pos <- credits[["Australian rule reductions (Mt)"]] > 0
rule_out <- credits$Year %in% natural_years
rule_worst <- which.min(credits[["Australian rule reductions (Mt)"]])

# Australia's second step for British Columbia: a nationally natural year counts as natural in the province only
# when the province's burned area exceeds its own mean over the same 13 years by one standard deviation
bc_burned <- dplyr::filter(burned, province == "BC")
bc_base <- bc_burned$hectares[bc_burned$year %in% years13]
bc_natural_years <- intersect(natural_years, bc_burned$year[bc_burned$hectares > mean(bc_base) + stats::sd(bc_base)])
bc_accounts <- dplyr::mutate(bc_accounts, rule = dplyr::if_else(year %in% bc_natural_years, human, net))
bc_level_rule <- sum(bc_accounts$rule[bc_accounts$year <= 2016]) / 5
bc_credits <- bc_credits |>
  dplyr::mutate(`Australian rule emissions (Mt)` = round(bc_accounts$rule[bc_accounts$year >= 2017], 1),
                `Australian rule reductions (Mt)` = round(bc_level_rule - bc_accounts$rule[bc_accounts$year >= 2017], 1))
bc_rule_pos <- bc_credits[["Australian rule reductions (Mt)"]] > 0
bc_rule_worst <- which.min(bc_credits[["Australian rule reductions (Mt)"]])
bc_threshold_ha <- mean(bc_base) + stats::sd(bc_base)
bc_ha <- \(y) bc_burned$hectares[bc_burned$year == y]

ci <- c(0.10, 0.20, 0.30, 0.50, 0.75, 1.00, 1.50, 2.00)
deductions <- data.frame(
  `Uncertainty, 90% interval half width (%)` = ci * 100,
  `Uncertainty deduction (%)` = round(100 * trees_uncertainty(ci), 1),
  `Kept, 25% buffer (%)` = round(100 * kept(ci), 1),
  `Kept, 5% buffer (%)` = round(100 * kept(ci, "1,2,3"), 1),
  `Kept, 30% buffer after a reversal (%)` = round(100 * kept(ci, after_reversal = TRUE), 1),
  check.names = FALSE)

set.seed(42)
sd_mt <- 16.6 * (44 / 12) / 1.96

simulate_reductions <- function(reference, emissions, n = 10000) {
  level <- rowMeans(matrix(rep(reference, each = n) +
                             stats::rnorm(n * length(reference), 0, sd_mt), nrow = n))
  level - (emissions + stats::rnorm(n, 0, sd_mt))
}

monte_carlo <- function(reference, series) {
  do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(series)), function(k) {
    draws <- simulate_reductions(reference, series$emissions[k])
    half <- (stats::quantile(draws, 0.95) - stats::quantile(draws, 0.05)) / 2
    data.frame(Year = series$year[k], mean = mean(draws), half = half,
               ci = half / abs(mean(draws)))
  }))
}

reference_split <- accounts$human[accounts$reference]
reference_whole <- accounts$net[accounts$reference]

mc_split <- monte_carlo(reference_split,
  data.frame(year = credits$Year, emissions = credits[["Disaggregated emissions (Mt)"]]))
mc_whole <- monte_carlo(reference_whole,
  data.frame(year = credits$Year, emissions = credits[["Undisaggregated emissions (Mt)"]]))
mc_rule <- monte_carlo(accounts$rule[accounts$reference],
  data.frame(year = credits$Year, emissions = credits[["Australian rule emissions (Mt)"]]))

blank_if_negative <- function(value, mean_reduction) ifelse(mean_reduction > 0, value, NA)

uncertainty <- data.frame(
  Year = mc_split$Year,
  `Disaggregated reductions (Mt)` = round(mc_split$mean, 1),
  `Disaggregated interval (% of mean)` = blank_if_negative(round(100 * mc_split$ci), mc_split$mean),
  `Disaggregated deduction (%)` = blank_if_negative(round(100 * trees_uncertainty(mc_split$ci), 1), mc_split$mean),
  `Undisaggregated reductions (Mt)` = round(mc_whole$mean, 1),
  `Undisaggregated interval (% of mean)` = blank_if_negative(round(100 * mc_whole$ci), mc_whole$mean),
  `Australian rule reductions (Mt)` = round(mc_rule$mean, 1),
  `Australian rule interval (% of mean)` = blank_if_negative(round(100 * mc_rule$ci), mc_rule$mean),
  `Australian rule deduction (%)` = blank_if_negative(round(100 * trees_uncertainty(mc_rule$ci), 1), mc_rule$mean),
  check.names = FALSE)

over <- uncertainty[["Disaggregated deduction (%)"]] > 100
banked <- ifelse(mc_split$mean > 0, 100 * purrr::map2_dbl(mc_split$ci, mc_split$Year > min(credits$Year[!split_pos]), \(ci, after) kept(ci, after_reversal = after)), NA)

msd <- \(x) sprintf("%.1f ± %.1f Mt CO~2~e a year (95 per cent confidence interval %.1f to %.1f)",
                    mean(x), stats::sd(x), stats::t.test(x)$conf.int[1], stats::t.test(x)$conf.int[2])
province <- dplyr::filter(eccc, region == "BC")

# Share of the annual error common to the reference years and the crediting year. A shared error cancels in
# the difference, the ground on which ART TREES excludes model error. The draws above share none. Under the
# normal model a shared share rho leaves the mean reduction and scales its half width by sqrt(1 - rho).
after <- credits$Year > min(credits$Year[!split_pos])
shared <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c(0, 0.5, 0.9, 0.99), function(rho) {
  ci <- mc_split$ci * sqrt(1 - rho)
  data.frame(`Shared share` = rho,
             `Interval, lowest (%)` = round(100 * min(ci[split_pos])),
             `Interval, highest (%)` = round(100 * max(ci[split_pos])),
             `Years keeping a credit` = sum(purrr::map2_dbl(ci, after, \(h, a) kept(h, after_reversal = a))[split_pos] > 0),
             check.names = FALSE)
}))
sh <- function(share, column) shared[[column]][shared[["Shared share"]] == share]
# The shared share at which every positive year keeps a credit, solved from the same scaling
rho_needed <- max(1 - (purrr::map_dbl(after[split_pos], \(a) break_even(after_reversal = a)) / mc_split$ci[split_pos])^2)

# Deduction the standard allows at the end of a crediting period, on the summed reference emissions minus the
# summed crediting period emissions, with the same independent draws
simulate_period <- function(reference, emissions, n = 10000) {
  level <- rowMeans(matrix(rep(reference, each = n) + stats::rnorm(n * length(reference), 0, sd_mt), nrow = n))
  total <- length(emissions) * level -
    rowSums(matrix(rep(emissions, each = n) + stats::rnorm(n * length(emissions), 0, sd_mt), nrow = n))
  half <- unname((stats::quantile(total, 0.95) - stats::quantile(total, 0.05)) / 2)
  c(total = mean(total), half = half, ci = half / abs(mean(total)))
}
period_split <- simulate_period(reference_split, credits[["Disaggregated emissions (Mt)"]])
period_rule <- simulate_period(accounts$rule[accounts$reference], credits[["Australian rule emissions (Mt)"]])
period_deduction <- period_split[["total"]] * trees_uncertainty(period_split[["ci"]])
yearly_deduction <- sum(mc_split$mean[split_pos] * trees_uncertainty(mc_split$ci[split_pos]))

# Approach 1 of the uncertainty chapter on the Tier 1 forest fire estimate: the relative uncertainty of a product
# is the square root of the sum of the squared relative uncertainties, each half a 95 per cent interval
u_term <- function(sd, mean) 1.96 * sd / mean
u_fuel <- u_term(table_2_4$se[1:2], table_2_4$fuel[1:2])
u_ef <- u_term(table_2_5$co2_sd[1], table_2_5$co2[1])
u_forest <- sqrt(u_fuel^2 + u_ef^2)
co2_2023 <- forest[["CO2 (kt)"]][forest$Year == 2023] / 1000
```

# Abstract {.unnumbered}

Canada reported its managed forest with natural disturbance disaggregated from human activity, as cited in the 2019 Refinement to the guidelines of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change. Whether it decided the credit a country could claim had not been tested. This study ran Canada's 2026 inventory through ART TREES, the standard of the Architecture for REDD+ Transactions, for the crediting years 2017 to 2024, with and without the disaggregation. A third account followed Australia's rule, which excluded natural disturbance only in fire years above a threshold. With the disaggregation, Canada showed reductions in `r sum(split_pos)` of `r nrow(credits)` crediting years, totalling `r round(sum(credits[["Disaggregated reductions (Mt)"]][split_pos]), 1)` million tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent. Without it, emissions exceeded the crediting level by `r format(abs(credits[["Undisaggregated reductions (Mt)"]][worst]), big.mark = ",")` million tonnes in `r credits$Year[worst]`. Australia's rule gave Canada `r round(sum(credits[["Australian rule reductions (Mt)"]][rule_pos]), 1)` million tonnes, `r round(sum(credits[["Australian rule reductions (Mt)"]][rule_pos]) / sum(credits[["Disaggregated reductions (Mt)"]][split_pos]), 1)` times its reported account, because ordinary fire years in the reference period raised the crediting level. The disaggregated account stayed uncertain by more than its own size, with deductions of `r format(min(uncertainty[["Disaggregated deduction (%)"]], na.rm = TRUE), big.mark = ",")` to `r format(max(uncertainty[["Disaggregated deduction (%)"]], na.rm = TRUE), big.mark = ",")` per cent. Nothing was left to issue once uncertainty reached `r round(100 * break_even())` per cent. Every positive year kept a credit only when more than `r round(100 * rho_needed, 1)` per cent of the model error was shared between years. Crediting standards relying on the disaggregation therefore needed a stated record length and regrowth period. They also needed to exclude only the part of an extreme fire year's emissions above those of an ordinary year. The uncertainty deduction had to be taken on gross emissions and removals rather than on a net near zero.

# Introduction

National greenhouse gas inventories reported the land sector on the assumption that every emission and removal on managed land was caused by people [@kurz2018quantifying]. Managed land thereby stood in for human activity, and the 2019 Refinement to the IPCC Guidelines called this assumption the managed land proxy, abbreviated there as MLP. In Canada's managed forest, the assumption added the emissions and later removals of fire and insects to those of harvest and regrowth [@kurz2018quantifying]. Those were large and varied widely between years, and so hid the effect of management in the reported trend [@kurz2018quantifying]. The Refinement took Canada's series for 1990 to 2016 as its example and offered "an approach that countries can apply on a voluntary basis within the MLP in order to indicate those emissions and removals considered to result from human activity, and those that are understood to result from natural disturbances" [@ogle2019generic]. The approach assumed that the carbon dioxide released would "be balanced by subsequent removals across the landscape at some future point in time" [@ogle2019generic].

The effect of the assumption in Canada was known before the Refinement. The Carbon Budget Model of the Canadian Forest Sector (CBM-CFS3) was run with future fire and insect outbreaks drawn at random [@kurz2008risk]. It projected the managed forest as a net source over 2008 to 2012, the first Kyoto commitment period [@kurz2008risk]. The projection ran from 30 to 245 Mt CO~2~e a year, the two ends set by how much fire and insect damage the draws produced [@kurz2008risk]. The 215 Mt spread equalled nearly 30 per cent of Canada's emissions in 2005 [@kurz2008risk]. Those outbreaks, the growing effect of natural disturbance and the Protocol's accounting rules led Canada to choose not to count forest management under the Kyoto Protocol [@kurz2008risk]. Canada's 2017 inventory then divided the managed forest into land dominated by natural disturbance and the rest, two parts that summed to the net emissions of the whole [@kurz2018quantifying]. A burned stand stayed in the natural disturbance part until it had enough wood to be worth cutting [@kurz2018quantifying]. That age was 60 years nationally in 2017 and later 60 to 100 years by region [@kurz2024revised]. A revised harvest record for 1889 to 1989 moved 34 million hectares into the natural disturbance part [@kurz2024revised]. That cut the human sink reported for 1990 by 113 Mt CO~2~e, or 56 per cent, without any change in the forest [@kurz2024revised]. Read from the same inventory tables, forestry was a net source of 90.8 Mt CO~2~e a year over 2005 to 2021, against a reported sink of 4.7 Mt [@bysouth2024high]. The authors explained the difference by the treatment of wildfire as natural [@bysouth2024high].

Other countries separated natural from human emissions by other routes. The United States divided forest carbon change between growth, land use change and natural disturbances such as fire [@woodall2015forest]. Australia classed a whole fire season as natural when national fire emissions exceeded the mean of a 2000 to 2012 baseline by two standard deviations [@bowman2023wildfire]. A state's burned area then had to exceed its own mean by one standard deviation [@bowman2023wildfire]. European forest carbon uptake in 2020 to 2023 was 17 to 27 per cent below its 1990 to 2019 average in every dataset compared [@linscheid2026forest]. In North America over 2010 to 2019, inventories, atmospheric inversions and process models disagreed on the net source, partly through what each counted as human [@poulter2026north]. Countries together reported a net land sink of 1.6 Gt CO~2~ a year over 2000 to 2020 [@grassi2022carbon]. FAOSTAT, the statistical database of the Food and Agriculture Organization, estimated a net source of 1.1 Gt over the same years [@grassi2022carbon].

In the Kyoto period, factoring out natural and indirect human effects was already treated as a requirement of accounting that tied credits to human activity. @canadell2007factoring set out five ways to do it, from longer accounting periods to national baselines. A review of the rules from Kyoto to Paris concluded that "factoring out direct human-induced from indirect human-induced and natural impacts on managed lands" was among the requirements "not sufficiently secured by currently discussed accounting rules" [@krug2018accounting]. The forest reference levels of the European Union, the projected baselines its members were judged against, credited harvest increases that policy assumed and that never took place [@grassi2018science].

Canada's reported figures came from one model, CBM-CFS3, the core of a national reporting system [@kurz2018quantifying]. The system used a Tier 3 method, the most detailed of the three the IPCC set out [@kurz2018quantifying]. The model grew each stand along a yield curve of wood volume against age and reset its age after a stand-replacing disturbance [@kurz2018quantifying]. It moved the carbon of each stand through a disturbance matrix for each type of disturbance, a table of the share of each pool moved [@kurz2018quantifying]. Over 71 years on a boreal landscape in eastern Canada, it underestimated the net biomass gain of undisturbed stands by 10 per cent [@bernier2010reconstructing]. Its fire matrices assumed that every fire burned at high severity [@thompson2026incorporating]. A sub-model built on mapped burn severity gave regional emissions typically 10 to 25 per cent lower [@thompson2026incorporating].

Whether a fire year counted as natural depended on the statistics of the fire regime, the pattern of how often and how widely a landscape burned. Under random fire the expected distribution of stand ages was the negative exponential, so that "the present age-class structure of such a forest is the key to its past fire history" [@wagner1978class]. The negative exponential and Weibull models became the standard descriptions of fire history [@johnson1985theory]. The fire cycle was defined as the time taken to burn an area equal to the area studied [@johnson1991climatically]. Fire cycles reported for Canada ran from 50 to 90 years in the Kananaskis watershed of Alberta [@johnson1991climatically] to 769 years in Newfoundland [@arsenault2016unravelling]. The estimates depended on the record behind them, since lengthening a Landsat series in Portugal from 22 to 31 years substantially changed the fitted Weibull parameters [@oliveira2011fire]. Charcoal records spanning millennia were therefore proposed as the baseline wherever recent fires were too few [@gavin2007forest].

A percentage uncertainty was the interval divided by the reported value, so a balance near zero had an uncertainty larger than itself whatever method produced the interval. Approach 1 of the 2019 Refinement combined uncertainties by formula and "theoretically requires that the standard deviation divided by the mean value is less than 0.3" [@paciornik2019uncertainties]. Approach 2, Monte Carlo simulation, "will be particularly appropriate to use when uncertainties are large, their distribution are non-Gaussian, and algorithms are complex functions" [@paciornik2019uncertainties]. The guidance itself advised caution "in cases where the point estimate is very small when compared with the size of the confidence interval" [@paciornik2019uncertainties]. The interval of Canada's own model was 32.2 Tg C a year wide, which @metsaranta2017uncertainty stated "cannot be meaningfully expressed in percentage terms because its range of possible values contains zero".

FAOSTAT gave every government an independent estimate of its fire emissions. The IPCC recommended it for checking an inventory's activity data, the measured quantities such as burned area, and its emission estimates. Its five page methodological note gave the equation, burned biomass multiplied by a default emission factor [@fao2025fires]. It did not give the code run in Google Earth Engine, the rule that allocated a fuel value to each pixel, or the meaning of keeping "only those pixels with a percentage uncertainty lower than 20 percent" [@fao2025fires]. It set the emissions of fires in organic soils to zero outside Southeast Asia, publishing the full values in a separate table [@fao2025fires]. Independent fire estimates disagreed widely, four satellite burned area datasets for Siberia differing up to fivefold [@kukavskaya2013fire].

What the disaggregation was worth was set by the crediting standard, the rules under which the reported reductions of a country or province became credits. The standard here was that of the Architecture for REDD+ Transactions, The REDD+ Environmental Excellence Standard, cited as ART TREES [@art2021trees]. ART TREES stated that "only anthropogenic emissions shall be considered, and IPCC guidance shall be adhered to on any exclusion of non-anthropogenic emissions" [@art2021trees]. Its 2025 draft added that natural disturbances "may be excluded if they are 'non-anthropogenic events or non-anthropogenic circumstances that cause significant emissions and are beyond the control of, and not materially influenced by a country'" [@art2025trees3; @ogle2019generic]. The uncertainty deduction multiplied gross reductions and removals by an adjustment factor, 0.524417 divided by 1.645006 times the half width of the 90 per cent confidence interval [@art2021trees]. That interval came from 10,000 Monte Carlo iterations [@art2021trees]. The buffer withheld 25 per cent of the same quantity, or 5 per cent where three mitigating factors were met [@art2021trees]. A reversal, any year after credits were issued in which reported emissions rose above the crediting level, raised the buffer by 5 percentage points for five years [@art2021trees].

No study found had run the account of a country or province through a crediting standard both with and without the disaggregation. The nearest compared Canada's reported series under different divisions of the managed forest [@kurz2024revised; @bysouth2024high]. Others compared national inventories with independent estimates [@pilli2016modellinga; @grassi2022carbon], or mapped reversal risk without reference to an inventory [@wu2026global]. This study therefore tested the natural disturbance approach of the 2019 Refinement on Canada and British Columbia over 1990 to 2024, the period of the 2026 national inventory. The objective was to compare what each reported, and what each could have been credited under ART TREES, with and without the approach, and under Australia's rule. Because the Refinement set no length for the record behind a natural disturbance test, baselines of 13, 20 and 30 years were compared. The fire emissions FAOSTAT published for Canada were then rebuilt from its stated method and compared with what Canada reported.

# Materials and Methods

## Data sources

Six datasets were read. Canada's inventory came as Table 6-1 of the 2026 National Inventory Report, 1990 to 2024, from Environment and Climate Change Canada (ECCC). Its fire polygons came from the Canadian National Fire Database of Natural Resources Canada (NRCan), 1990 to 2024. FAOSTAT supplied its Emissions from Fires domain, 1990 to 2024, and the AllFires_OrganicSoils table FAO released beside it, 1990 to 2021. The domain itself was built on two MODIS products, MCD64A1 burned area for 2000 to 2024 and MCD12Q1 land cover for 2001 to 2023.

## IPCC method

The disaggregation followed section 2.6 of Volume 4, Chapter 2 of the 2019 Refinement [@ogle2019generic]. That section stated that "Voluntary disaggregation of the total of emissions and removals in the MLP into those that are associated with human effects and those due to natural disturbances may provide a clearer picture of the impact of management activities" [@ogle2019generic]. Its footnote 9 stated that "Disaggregating means that an estimate is separated into its component parts" [@ogle2019generic]. The total stayed reported, with the two parts beside it [@ogle2019generic]. The Refinement set no length for the record behind a natural disturbance test, the gap tested below. Canada divided the land into two parts, as set out below, and Australia divided the years, as set out under the natural disturbance rule.

## Canadian inventory

Canada reported its land use sector in Table 6-1 of the 2026 national inventory report [@eccc2026nir]. The table gave the net emissions of seven categories and their total (@fig-inventory). The categories were forest land, cropland, grassland, wetlands, settlements, other land and harvested wood products. Beneath the total it gave one more line, natural disturbances, which the table marked as "Not a reporting category" and "provided solely for transparency purposes" [@eccc2026nir]. That line held the net balance of emissions and removals from natural disturbances in the managed forest, and the total above it left that balance out. Every wildfire in the managed forest went to the natural disturbance line, whatever its cause [@eccc2026nir]. It stayed there with its regrowth until the stand reached the age at which it had enough wood to be worth cutting [@eccc2026nir]. Fires that killed a fifth or less of a mature stand, slash burning and prescribed burning stayed in the total [@eccc2026nir].

```{r}
#| label: fig-inventory
#| fig-cap: "Net emissions of Canada's land use sector by category, 1990 to 2024, from Table 6-1 of the 2026 inventory. The lower panel is the natural disturbance line the table shows beside the total but leaves out of it."

# Table 6-1, Net Greenhouse Gas Flux Estimates in the Land Use, Land-Use Change and Forestry Sector,
# All Inventory Years, by province and territory, Environment and Climate Change Canada,
# National Inventory Report 1990-2024
# https://data-donnees.az.ec.gc.ca/data/substances/monitor/canada-s-official-greenhouse-gas-inventory/E-LULUCF/?lang=en
if (!file.exists("02.inputs/eccc/lulucf-2026-categories.csv")) {
  if (!file.exists("02.inputs/eccc/raw/table-6-1.xlsx")) {
    dir.create("02.inputs/eccc/raw", showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
    download.file(paste0("https://data-donnees.az.ec.gc.ca/api/file?path=", URLencode("/substances/monitor/canada-s-official-greenhouse-gas-inventory/E-LULUCF/NIR2026_Table 6-1_All_Years_PTs.xlsx", reserved = TRUE)), "02.inputs/eccc/raw/table-6-1.xlsx", mode = "wb")
  }
  sheets <- readxl::excel_sheets("02.inputs/eccc/raw/table-6-1.xlsx")
  readxl::read_excel("02.inputs/eccc/raw/table-6-1.xlsx", sheet = grep("NATIONAL$", sheets, value = TRUE), skip = 3, col_types = "text", .name_repair = "unique_quiet") |>
    dplyr::transmute(category = dplyr::case_when(grepl("TOTAL", ...1) ~ "Sector total", grepl("^Natural disturbances", ...2) ~ "Natural disturbances", grepl("^[a-g]\\.$", ...1) ~ ...2),
                     dplyr::across(dplyr::matches("^[0-9]{4}$"), as.numeric)) |>
    dplyr::filter(!is.na(category)) |>
    tidyr::pivot_longer(-category, names_to = "year", values_to = "kt", names_transform = as.integer) |>
    readr::write_csv("02.inputs/eccc/lulucf-2026-categories.csv", na = "")
}

categories <- readr::read_csv("02.inputs/eccc/lulucf-2026-categories.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(kt)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(mt = kt / 1000,
                panel = factor(dplyr::if_else(category == "Natural disturbances", "Natural disturbances, shown beside the total and left out of it", "Reported categories and their total"), levels = c("Reported categories and their total", "Natural disturbances, shown beside the total and left out of it")),
                category = factor(category, levels = c("Forest Land", "Cropland", "Grassland", "Wetlands", "Settlements", "Harvested Wood Products", "Sector total", "Natural disturbances")))

ggplot2::ggplot(categories, ggplot2::aes(year, mt, colour = category)) +
  ggplot2::geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linewidth = 0.3, colour = "grey60") +
  ggplot2::geom_line() +
  ggplot2::facet_wrap(~panel, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  ggplot2::scale_colour_manual(values = unname(grDevices::palette.colors(8, "Okabe-Ito"))) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = NULL, y = expression("Net emissions (Mt CO"[2]*"e)"), colour = NULL) +
  th +
  ggplot2::theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

Two series were read from the table for Canada and for British Columbia. The first was the reported total, the disaggregated account. The second was that total plus the natural disturbance line, the account without disaggregation. Both came from Canada's National Forest Carbon Monitoring, Accounting and Reporting System [@kurz2018quantifying]. Its core model, CBM-CFS3, grew each stand along a yield curve and moved its carbon through a disturbance matrix [@kurz2018quantifying]. Its fire matrices assumed that every fire burned at high severity [@thompson2026incorporating]. British Columbia's share of the area burned in Canada each year was computed from the Canadian National Fire Database. The database held the fire polygons of every provincial, territorial and federal agency. The two accounts were compared over 1990 to 2024 by the mean and standard deviation of their annual net emissions, following @kurz2024revised. The crediting arithmetic was then applied to the years from 2012.

## Natural disturbance rule

Canada's inventory, as set out above, left the natural disturbance line out of its total in every year. Australia's inventory instead left fire out only in a year its rule classed as natural. That rule was applied here to FAOSTAT's forest fire carbon dioxide series for Canada, 2001 to 2024, in the form Australia used [@bowman2023wildfire]. A year counted as natural when its fire emissions exceeded the baseline mean by two standard deviations. The rule was run on baselines of 13, 20 and 30 years, the first being the length Australia used, 2000 to 2012.

The shortest baseline, 13 years, was then used to build a third account from the two lines of Canada's inventory. In a year the rule classed as natural, the natural disturbance line was left out, as in the account Canada reported. In every other year it was kept, as in the undisaggregated account. Canada published that line once a year, combining the year's fire and insect emissions with the regrowth of earlier disturbances. The third account therefore left out the regrowth of earlier fires in a natural year and kept it in other years. Australia's inventory instead kept the land of an excluded fire "disaggregated, tracked, and reported on separately from the point in time it was disturbed until the time forest carbon has returned to its original state" [@bowman2023wildfire]. For British Columbia the rule's second step was also applied. Under it an anomalous season counted as natural in a state only if "the area burned in each state and territory exceeds by one standard deviation the average area burned during the 2000–2012 baseline" [@bowman2023wildfire]. The province's burned area was taken from the Canadian National Fire Database over the same 13 years, 2001 to 2013.

## ART TREES crediting

The crediting level was the mean emissions of the five year reference period, 2012 to 2016 [@art2021trees]. The reduction in each crediting year, 2017 to 2024, was that level minus the emissions reported for the year [@art2021trees]. Both were computed on the disaggregated account, the total Canada reported, on that total plus the natural disturbance line, and on the account built under Australia's rule. The two deductions were implemented as the standard wrote them. The uncertainty deduction took the adjustment factor of Equation 11 of ART TREES, and the buffer took the contribution of its Table 2 [@art2021trees].

## Account uncertainty

The uncertainty of each account followed Approach 2 of the Refinement's uncertainty chapter, Monte Carlo simulation [@paciornik2019uncertainties]. The chapter stated that Approach 2 "will be particularly appropriate to use when uncertainties are large, their distribution are non-Gaussian, and algorithms are complex functions" [@paciornik2019uncertainties]. The published uncertainty of CBM-CFS3 was a 95 per cent interval 32.2 Tg C a year wide, 16.6 above its median and 15.6 below [@metsaranta2017uncertainty]. It was converted to a standard deviation by dividing the larger side, 16.6 Tg C, by 1.96. That standard deviation was applied to every annual value of every account. It assumed the model was no more certain of a megafire year than of a quiet one. Each run drew the five reference years and the crediting year from normal distributions with that standard deviation. Ten thousand runs gave the distribution of each year's reduction. The half width of its 90 per cent interval, divided by the mean reduction, was the uncertainty on which ART TREES set its deduction.

Those draws treated the error of each year as independent of every other. ART TREES excluded model error on the opposite premise, that such error was "consistent between emissions in the crediting level and crediting periods" [@art2021trees]. The share of the error variance common to all years was therefore varied. Under the normal model a shared share left the mean reduction unchanged and scaled its half width by the square root of the unshared share. The intervals at shares of 0.5, 0.9 and 0.99 followed from the independent draws. The share at which every positive year kept a credit was solved from the same relation.

The standard also allowed a deduction at the end of a crediting period "based on the summed uncertainty of gross emission reductions and removals during the total period" [@art2021trees]. That total was "summed reference emissions minus summed crediting period emissions or removals" [@art2021trees], simulated here with the same draws for the disaggregated account and the account under Australia's rule. Its 90 per cent half width over its mean gave the period uncertainty, and the deduction on the total was compared with the sum of the yearly deductions.

## FAOSTAT check

FAOSTAT, the statistical database of the Food and Agriculture Organization, was examined last, as the tool governments use to check their fire emissions. It published country totals without the pixel data or the code behind them, so a government could not rebuild its own figure. The method was taken from the five page methodological note that FAO published with the domain [@fao2025fires].

FAOSTAT computed each pixel's fire emissions as its burned area multiplied by the fuel consumption of its vegetation type and by each gas's default emission factor [@fao2025fires]. It summed them to countries and published them for forest fires, savanna fires and fires in organic soils. The note stated that forest fire carbon dioxide was left out because the FAOSTAT Forests domain counted it [@fao2025fires]. Savanna fire carbon dioxide was left out on the assumption that regrowth balanced it within a year [@fao2025fires]. The domain nonetheless returned carbon dioxide for forest fires from 2001, and those values were reported here. Each year's value was compared with the value Canada submitted for the same item, which FAOSTAT published in the same domain. That followed comparisons of FAOSTAT with national inventories [@grassi2022carbon; @nyawira2024pantropical] and of an independent model with European inventories [@pilli2016modellinga]. The coefficients FAOSTAT applied were then recovered from its published values for Canada. Biomass burned divided by burned area gave the fuel consumed per hectare. Each emission divided by biomass burned gave the emission factor per kilogram of dry matter. Both were compared with Tables 2.4 and 2.5 of the 2006 Guidelines that the note cited [@aalde2006generic; @fao2025fires].

The uncertainty of the Tier 1 forest fire estimate was then propagated by Approach 1 of the uncertainty chapter from the spreads the two tables printed [@paciornik2019uncertainties]. Each term's uncertainty was 1.96 times its standard error or standard deviation over its mean, the chapter's form for a 95 per cent interval [@paciornik2019uncertainties]. The terms combined as the square root of the sum of their squares, Equation 3.1 of the chapter. The chapter called that rule "approximate for all random variables" and "reasonably accurate as long as the percentage uncertainty is less than approximately 30%" [@paciornik2019uncertainties]. The fuel took the boreal and other temperate rows of Table 2.4, between which FAOSTAT's values lay. The emission factor took the savanna and grassland row of Table 2.5 that it applied. The burned area carried no stated uncertainty, so the result was a lower bound.

The domain was retrieved for Canada through the FAOSTAT application programming interface and cached. The withheld organic soil values were read from the `AllFires_OrganicSoils` table released beside it.

# Results

## Reported national emissions

```{r}
#| label: fig-accounts
#| fig-cap: "Net emissions of the land use sector for Canada and British Columbia, 1990 to 2024, under two accounts. The disaggregated account is the total Canada reports, and the undisaggregated account is that total plus the natural disturbance line."

eccc |>
  dplyr::mutate(region = factor(dplyr::if_else(region == "BC", "British Columbia", region), levels = c("Canada", "British Columbia"))) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(c(human, net), names_to = "account", values_to = "mt") |>
  dplyr::mutate(account = dplyr::if_else(account == "human", "Disaggregated, as reported", "Undisaggregated")) |>
  ggplot2::ggplot(ggplot2::aes(year, mt, linetype = account)) +
  ggplot2::geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linewidth = 0.3, colour = "grey60") +
  ggplot2::geom_line() +
  ggplot2::facet_wrap(~region, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  ggplot2::labs(x = NULL, y = expression("Net emissions (Mt CO"[2]*"e)"), linetype = NULL) +
  th +
  ggplot2::theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

Disaggregating natural disturbance cut the standard deviation of Canada's annual land use emissions from `r round(stats::sd(national$net))` to `r round(stats::sd(national$human))` Mt CO~2~e over 1990 to 2024, a factor of `r round(stats::sd(national$net) / stats::sd(national$human), 1)` (@fig-accounts). The account Canada reported averaged `r msd(national$human)`. Without the disaggregation the same land averaged `r msd(national$net)`. In 2023 Canada reported `r national$human[national$year == 2023]` Mt where the undisaggregated account showed `r format(round(national$net[national$year == 2023]), big.mark = ",")` Mt. British Columbia's reported account averaged `r msd(province$human)`. Without the disaggregation it averaged `r msd(province$net)`, a standard deviation `r round(stats::sd(province$net) / stats::sd(province$human), 1)` times larger. In 2023 the province reported `r province$human[province$year == 2023]` Mt against `r round(province$net[province$year == 2023])` Mt.

## Natural fire years

The baseline length moved the threshold but not the classification. Lengthening the baseline from 13 to 20 years raised the threshold from `r format(baselines[["Threshold (kt)"]][1], big.mark = ",")` to `r format(baselines[["Threshold (kt)"]][2], big.mark = ",")` kilotonnes of carbon dioxide, a rise of `r round(100 * (baselines[["Threshold (kt)"]][2] / baselines[["Threshold (kt)"]][1] - 1))` per cent. Both lengths classed the same `r length(strsplit(baselines[["Years classified natural"]][1], ", ")[[1]])` years as natural, `r baselines[["Years classified natural"]][1]`. A 30 year baseline could not be run, because the FAOSTAT series covered only `r nrow(forest_co2)` years derived from observations, 2001 to 2024.

## Crediting Canada

```{r}
#| label: tbl-credits
#| tbl-cap: "Emissions and reductions for Canada's managed land under three accounts, 2017 to 2024, on a 2012 to 2016 reference period. The Australian rule account leaves out the natural disturbance line only in the years the 13 year baseline classes as natural. A negative reduction is emissions above the crediting level, a reversal under ART TREES."

readr::write_csv(credits, "03.outputs/TBL/tbl-credits.csv")
fmt_tbl(credits)
```


The disaggregation decided whether there was anything to credit. On the account Canada reported, reductions were positive in `r sum(split_pos)` of the `r nrow(credits)` crediting years and summed to `r round(sum(credits[["Disaggregated reductions (Mt)"]][split_pos]), 1)` Mt of carbon dioxide equivalent. The `r sum(!split_pos)` years below the crediting level were `r credits$Year[!split_pos][1]` at `r credits[["Disaggregated reductions (Mt)"]][!split_pos][1]` Mt and `r credits$Year[!split_pos][2]` at `r credits[["Disaggregated reductions (Mt)"]][!split_pos][2]` Mt. Without the disaggregation, reductions were positive in only `r sum(whole_pos)` years. The shortfall in `r credits$Year[worst]` alone reached `r format(abs(credits[["Undisaggregated reductions (Mt)"]][worst]), big.mark = ",")` Mt, `r round(abs(credits[["Undisaggregated reductions (Mt)"]][worst]) / sum(credits[["Disaggregated reductions (Mt)"]][split_pos]))` times every reduction the disaggregated account achieved over the period (@tbl-credits).

The reversal rule of ART TREES retired buffer credits equal to the lower of the emissions above the crediting level or every credit issued [@art2021trees]. An undisaggregated account of this land therefore exhausted its buffer in `r credits$Year[which(!whole_pos)[1]]` and again in each later year that emissions exceeded the level.

Australia's rule gave more credit than either account. It left out the natural disturbance line in `r paste(natural_years[natural_years <= 2016], collapse = " and ")`, the only reference year it classed as natural, and kept it in the other four. That set the crediting level at `r round(level_rule, 1)` Mt of carbon dioxide equivalent, against `r round(level_split, 1)` Mt on the account Canada reported and `r round(level_whole, 1)` Mt without the disaggregation. The `r sum(rule_out)` crediting years the rule classed as natural then fell well below that level. Reductions were therefore positive in `r sum(rule_pos)` of the `r nrow(credits)` years and summed to `r round(sum(credits[["Australian rule reductions (Mt)"]][rule_pos]), 1)` Mt, `r round(sum(credits[["Australian rule reductions (Mt)"]][rule_pos]) / sum(credits[["Disaggregated reductions (Mt)"]][split_pos]), 1)` times the total on the account Canada reported. The shortfalls fell in the years the rule classed as ordinary, the largest in `r credits$Year[rule_worst]` at `r abs(credits[["Australian rule reductions (Mt)"]][rule_worst])` Mt (@tbl-credits).

## Crediting British Columbia

```{r}
#| label: tbl-bc
#| tbl-cap: "Emissions and reductions for British Columbia under three accounts, 2017 to 2024, on a 2012 to 2016 reference period, from the provincial lines of the national inventory. The burned area share is the province's share of the area burned in Canada. The Australian rule account leaves out the natural disturbance line only in years that pass both the national and the provincial test."

readr::write_csv(bc_credits, "03.outputs/TBL/tbl-bc.csv")
fmt_tbl(bc_credits)
```


British Columbia followed the national pattern more sharply. The province had `r bc_credits[["Burned area share (%)"]][bc_credits$Year == 2018]` per cent of the area burned in Canada in 2018 and `r bc_credits[["Burned area share (%)"]][bc_credits$Year == 2023]` per cent in 2023. On the disaggregated account its reductions were positive in `r sum(bc_split_pos)` of the `r nrow(bc_credits)` crediting years, summing to `r round(sum(bc_credits[["Disaggregated reductions (Mt)"]][bc_split_pos]), 1)` Mt of carbon dioxide equivalent. Without the disaggregation they were positive in `r sum(bc_whole_pos)` years, and `r bc_credits$Year[bc_worst]` fell `r format(abs(bc_credits[["Undisaggregated reductions (Mt)"]][bc_worst]), big.mark = ",")` Mt below the crediting level (@tbl-bc).

Under Australia's rule the province's burned area exceeded its own threshold of `r format(round(bc_threshold_ha), big.mark = ",")` hectares in every year the national test marked. The same `r length(bc_natural_years)` years were therefore classed as natural. Reductions were positive in `r sum(bc_rule_pos)` of the `r nrow(bc_credits)` crediting years and summed to `r round(sum(bc_credits[["Australian rule reductions (Mt)"]][bc_rule_pos]), 1)` Mt, against `r round(sum(bc_credits[["Disaggregated reductions (Mt)"]][bc_split_pos]), 1)` Mt on the disaggregated account. The largest shortfall fell in `r bc_credits$Year[bc_rule_worst]`, at `r abs(bc_credits[["Australian rule reductions (Mt)"]][bc_rule_worst])` Mt. The national test classed that year as ordinary although British Columbia burned `r format(round(bc_ha(bc_credits$Year[bc_rule_worst])), big.mark = ",")` hectares, `r round(bc_ha(bc_credits$Year[bc_rule_worst]) / bc_threshold_ha, 1)` times its own threshold.

## Account uncertainty

```{r}
#| label: tbl-uncertainty
#| tbl-cap: "Reductions and their uncertainty for Canada under the three accounts, from 10,000 Monte Carlo draws. The interval is the 90 per cent interval ART TREES requires, its half width against the mean reduction, and the deduction is what the adjustment factor takes from it. A percentage is printed only where the mean reduction is positive."

readr::write_csv(uncertainty, "03.outputs/TBL/tbl-uncertainty.csv")
fmt_tbl(uncertainty)
```

In the crediting arithmetic the published interval was wider than the reductions it qualified. The model's own authors had reported that interval as `r round(32.2 * 44 / 12)` Mt of carbon dioxide equivalent wide around a median of `r round(-0.8 * 44 / 12, 1)` Mt [@metsaranta2017uncertainty]. Across the `r sum(!is.na(uncertainty[["Disaggregated interval (% of mean)"]]))` crediting years with a positive mean reduction, the interval of the disaggregated account ran from `r format(min(uncertainty[["Disaggregated interval (% of mean)"]], na.rm = TRUE), big.mark = ",")` to `r format(max(uncertainty[["Disaggregated interval (% of mean)"]], na.rm = TRUE), big.mark = ",")` per cent of its mean reduction. The implied uncertainty deduction ran from `r format(min(uncertainty[["Disaggregated deduction (%)"]], na.rm = TRUE), big.mark = ",")` to `r format(max(uncertainty[["Disaggregated deduction (%)"]], na.rm = TRUE), big.mark = ",")` per cent (@tbl-uncertainty). The disaggregation restored the sign of the account but left the credit uncertain by more than its own size. Under Australia's rule the interval ran from `r min(uncertainty[["Australian rule interval (% of mean)"]], na.rm = TRUE)` to `r max(uncertainty[["Australian rule interval (% of mean)"]], na.rm = TRUE)` per cent of the mean reduction and the deduction from `r min(uncertainty[["Australian rule deduction (%)"]], na.rm = TRUE)` to `r max(uncertainty[["Australian rule deduction (%)"]], na.rm = TRUE)` per cent. That was because its reductions were larger, not because its yearly emissions and removals were more certain.

The independent draws set the ceiling of that uncertainty. With half the error variance shared between the reference years and the crediting year, the interval of the disaggregated account ran from `r sh(0.5, "Interval, lowest (%)")` to `r format(sh(0.5, "Interval, highest (%)"), big.mark = ",")` per cent, and `r sh(0.5, "Years keeping a credit")` of the `r sum(split_pos)` positive years kept a credit. With 90 per cent shared it ran from `r sh(0.9, "Interval, lowest (%)")` to `r format(sh(0.9, "Interval, highest (%)"), big.mark = ",")` per cent and `r sh(0.9, "Years keeping a credit")` years kept one. With 99 per cent shared, `r sh(0.99, "Years keeping a credit")` years kept one. Every positive year kept a credit only when the shared share exceeded `r round(100 * rho_needed, 1)` per cent, which left each year's own error at `r round(100 * sqrt(1 - rho_needed), 1)` per cent of the published standard deviation.

## After the deductions

Because the two deductions were linear in the uncertainty, the uncertainty at which nothing was kept could be solved directly. On the default buffer it was `r round(100 * break_even())` per cent. With all three mitigating factors and the smallest buffer it was `r round(100 * break_even("1,2,3"))` per cent, and in the five years after a reversal `r round(100 * break_even(after_reversal = TRUE))` per cent.

The period deduction the standard allowed at the end of a crediting period did not change the outcome. Over the eight years the disaggregated account's total reduction was `r round(period_split[["total"]], 1)` Mt within a 90 per cent half width of `r round(period_split[["half"]])` Mt, `r round(100 * period_split[["ci"]])` per cent of its size. The deduction on that total was `r round(100 * trees_uncertainty(period_split[["ci"]]))` per cent, `r round(period_deduction, 1)` Mt against the `r round(yearly_deduction, 1)` Mt summed from the yearly deductions, and the buffer left nothing. The account under Australia's rule totalled `r round(period_rule[["total"]], 1)` Mt at `r round(100 * period_rule[["ci"]])` per cent, a deduction of `r round(100 * trees_uncertainty(period_rule[["ci"]]), 1)` per cent against yearly deductions of `r min(uncertainty[["Australian rule deduction (%)"]], na.rm = TRUE)` to `r max(uncertainty[["Australian rule deduction (%)"]], na.rm = TRUE)` per cent. It kept `r round(100 * kept(period_rule[["ci"]]))` per cent of the total, `r round(period_rule[["total"]] * kept(period_rule[["ci"]]), 1)` Mt, on the default buffer.

## Canadian fire emissions

Forest fires in Canada released `r format(round(forest[["CO2 (kt)"]][forest$Year == 2023] / 1000), big.mark = ",")` Mt of carbon dioxide in 2023 on the FAOSTAT Tier 1 estimate. That was `r round(forest[["CO2 (kt)"]][forest$Year == 2023] / mean(forest[["CO2 (kt)"]][forest$Year < 2023]), 1)` times the mean of the earlier years and `r round(forest[["CO2 (kt)"]][forest$Year == 2023] / forest[["CO2 (kt)"]][forest$Year == 2020], 0)` times the quietest year, 2020, at `r format(round(forest[["CO2 (kt)"]][forest$Year == 2020] / 1000, 1), nsmall = 1)` Mt.

Across the `r nrow(gap)` years both sources reported, the FAOSTAT Tier 1 estimate was a median of `r round(median(gap$Ratio), 1)` times the value Canada submitted. The ratio ran from `r min(gap$Ratio)` times in `r gap$Year[which.min(gap$Ratio)]` to `r max(gap$Ratio)` times in `r gap$Year[which.max(gap$Ratio)]`.

Propagated by Approach 1 from the spreads of the two tables, the fuel term alone carried an uncertainty of `r round(100 * u_fuel[1])` to `r round(100 * u_fuel[2])` per cent and the emission factor `r round(100 * u_ef)` per cent. Combined they gave `r round(100 * u_forest[1])` to `r round(100 * u_forest[2])` per cent before any error in burned area. The 2023 estimate of `r round(co2_2023)` Mt therefore lay within `r round(co2_2023 * (1 - u_forest[1]))` to `r round(co2_2023 * (1 + u_forest[1]))` Mt on the boreal row, an interval that contained zero.

## FAOSTAT's coefficients

```{r}
#| label: tbl-coefficients
#| tbl-cap: "Fuel consumption and emission factors FAOSTAT applied to fires in Canada, 2001 to 2024, recovered from its published values. The fuel is biomass burned divided by burned area, and each emission factor is the emission divided by biomass burned. The last columns name the rows of IPCC Tables 2.4 and 2.5 that the values equal. Carbon dioxide is not reported for the savanna, grassland and shrubland items."

readr::write_csv(coefficients, "03.outputs/TBL/tbl-coefficients.csv")
fmt_tbl(coefficients)
```

FAOSTAT's published values for Canada showed which coefficients it had applied (@tbl-coefficients). Its biomass burned divided by its burned area gave `r sprintf("%.1f", min(used$fuel[used$item == "Other forest"]))` to `r sprintf("%.1f", max(used$fuel[used$item == "Other forest"]))` tonnes of dry matter per hectare for other forest. That range lay between the 41.0 of Table 2.4 for all boreal forest and the 50.4 for all other temperate forests [@aalde2006generic]. Its emissions divided by its biomass burned gave `r coefficients[["CO2 (g/kg)"]][coefficients$Item == "Other forest"]` g of carbon dioxide, `r coefficients[["CH4 (g/kg)"]][coefficients$Item == "Other forest"]` g of methane and `r coefficients[["N2O (g/kg)"]][coefficients$Item == "Other forest"]` g of nitrous oxide per kilogram of dry matter. These were the factors of Table 2.5 for savanna and grassland. The extra tropical forest row, which the table notes "includes all other forest types", gave `r format(table_2_5$co2[2], big.mark = ",")`, `r table_2_5$ch4[2]` and `r table_2_5$n2o[2]` [@aalde2006generic]. The methane FAOSTAT reported for Canada's forest fires was therefore `r round(100 * table_2_5$ch4[1] / table_2_5$ch4[2])` per cent of what its cited factors gave. The nitrous oxide was `r round(100 * table_2_5$n2o[1] / table_2_5$n2o[2])` per cent and the carbon dioxide `r round(100 * table_2_5$co2[1] / table_2_5$co2[2])` per cent. The domain also placed `r round(100 * sum(savanna_share[["Savanna fires"]]) / sum(savanna_share[["Savanna fires"]] + savanna_share[["Forest fires"]]))` per cent of the area it recorded as burned in Canada over 2001 to 2024 in its savanna, grassland and shrubland items. To these it applied the Table 2.4 values for savanna woodland and grassland burned in the mid or late dry season, `r table_2_4$fuel[3]` and `r table_2_4$fuel[4]` tonnes per hectare. It reported no carbon dioxide for them.

## Organic soil fires

Over the `r nrow(obs)` years of the satellite record, 2001 to 2021, fires in organic soils in Canada burned a mean of `r format(round(mean(obs[["Burned area (ha)"]])), big.mark = ",")` hectares a year. They released `r format(round(mean(obs[["CO2 (kt)"]])), big.mark = ",")` kilotonnes of carbon dioxide and `r format(round(mean(obs[["CH4 (kt)"]])), big.mark = ",")` kilotonnes of methane a year, none of which appeared in the FAOSTAT domain a government downloaded. The largest year was `r obs$Year[which.max(obs[["Burned area (ha)"]])]`, at `r format(round(max(obs[["Burned area (ha)"]])), big.mark = ",")` hectares and `r format(round(obs[["CO2 (kt)"]][which.max(obs[["Burned area (ha)"]])]), big.mark = ",")` kilotonnes of carbon dioxide. The smallest was `r obs$Year[which.min(obs[["Burned area (ha)"]])]`, at `r format(round(min(obs[["Burned area (ha)"]])), big.mark = ",")` hectares.

# Discussion

On the two lines of Canada's 2026 inventory, disaggregating natural disturbance decided whether an account existed to credit in 2017 to 2024. It did not make that account precise. The managed land of the country reported reductions in `r sum(split_pos)` of the `r nrow(credits)` years, totalling `r round(sum(credits[["Disaggregated reductions (Mt)"]][split_pos]), 1)` Mt of carbon dioxide equivalent. The same land without the disaggregation reported them in `r sum(whole_pos)` years and fell `r format(abs(credits[["Undisaggregated reductions (Mt)"]][worst]), big.mark = ",")` Mt short of its crediting level in 2023 alone. British Columbia, with `r bc_credits[["Burned area share (%)"]][bc_credits$Year == 2023]` per cent of the area burned in Canada that year, reversed in the same way. It reported `r round(sum(bc_credits[["Disaggregated reductions (Mt)"]][bc_split_pos]), 1)` Mt disaggregated against a shortfall of `r format(abs(bc_credits[["Undisaggregated reductions (Mt)"]][bc_worst]), big.mark = ",")` Mt. The disaggregation was therefore the condition on which a credit existed, rather than an adjustment to a reported number. Earlier work found the same dependence, in that the division rather than the forest moved Canada's reported balance under Kyoto and after the harvest revision [@kurz2008risk; @kurz2024revised; @bysouth2024high]. A standard that took the reported balance as its input passed the division straight into the credit.

The rest of this Discussion took in turn the uncertainty of a net near zero, the record and regrowth period, the natural disturbance rule and the fire emission method. The buffers and the changes that would close these gaps followed.

The disaggregated account kept part of its reductions in only `r sum(banked > 0, na.rm = TRUE)` of the `r sum(!is.na(banked))` years with a positive reduction, for an arithmetic rather than an ecological reason. An account whose emissions and removals nearly cancelled reported a percentage uncertainty far larger than either side of it. @paciornik2019uncertainties warned against interpreting that case. Canada's own inventory met the same limit in 2024. Its Forest Land carbon dioxide was a net of −1.9 Mt within a 95 per cent interval of −63 to 19 Mt. The inventory printed that interval as 3,100 and −1,100 per cent [@eccc2026nir]. Applied to the crediting equations, the published interval gave uncertainty deductions of `r format(min(uncertainty[["Disaggregated deduction (%)"]], na.rm = TRUE), big.mark = ",")` to `r format(max(uncertainty[["Disaggregated deduction (%)"]], na.rm = TRUE), big.mark = ",")` per cent. Those exceeded the reduction in `r sum(over, na.rm = TRUE)` of the `r sum(!is.na(over))` years with a positive reduction and fell below it only in `r paste(uncertainty$Year[which(!over)], collapse = " and ")`. In `r mc_split$Year[which(banked > 0)]` the account kept `r round(banked[which(banked > 0)], 1)` per cent of its reduction. That was after the uncertainty deduction and a buffer that the shortfall of `r min(credits$Year[!split_pos])` had raised to `r 100 * trees_buffer(after_reversal = TRUE)` per cent.

The standards differed in what such an interval cost. The adjustment factor of ART TREES rose with the interval without limit [@art2021trees]. The Forest Carbon Partnership Facility instead capped its uncertainty set-aside at 15 per cent [@fcpf2024buffer]. Under that cap a positive reduction kept at least `r round(100 * (1 - 0.15) * (1 - 0.40))` per cent of itself after both set-asides.

The length of the record mattered less to the classification than to the threshold. Lengthening the baseline from 13 to 20 years raised the threshold by `r round(100 * (baselines[["Threshold (kt)"]][2] / baselines[["Threshold (kt)"]][1] - 1))` per cent and marked the same `r length(strsplit(baselines[["Years classified natural"]][1], ", ")[[1]])` years. A 30 year baseline could not be tested because the satellite record covered only `r nrow(forest_co2)` years. Fire cycles in Canada ran from 50 to 769 years [@johnson1991climatically; @arsenault2016unravelling], so a baseline of 13 to 30 years sampled a small part of one cycle.

Of the three crediting documents read for this study, only Verra's tool set a record length, 100 years with no fewer than 20 [@verra2024nprt]. Canada applied no baseline at all. It reconstructed instead the cause of every stand for 1889 to 1989 [@kurz2024revised]. Each burned area then stayed on the natural disturbance line for the 60 to 100 years it took to regrow to a harvestable age [@kurz2024revised]. Australia tested fire seasons against a 13 year mean [@bowman2023wildfire]. The European example in the guidance used the 20 years before the base year and assumed 20 years of regrowth [@ogle2019generic]. Three inventories thus used three record lengths under guidance that set none. The regrowth half of the account also carried the model's 10 per cent underestimate of regrowth over 71 years [@bernier2010reconstructing].

The rule that classed a year as natural also decided how much was credited. On Canada's inventory, Australia's rule gave `r round(sum(credits[["Australian rule reductions (Mt)"]][rule_pos]), 1)` Mt of reductions over 2017 to 2024, `r round(sum(credits[["Australian rule reductions (Mt)"]][rule_pos]) / sum(credits[["Disaggregated reductions (Mt)"]][split_pos]), 1)` times the account Canada reported. The gain came from the crediting level rather than from the forest. The rule kept the natural disturbance line in four of the five reference years and then left all of it out of the crediting years it classed as natural. The fires of ordinary years therefore raised the level that an extreme year was measured against. The Kyoto Protocol provision avoided this by including a background level of natural disturbance emissions in the reference level. It allowed only "the emissions above the background level" to be excluded in a year that exceeded it [@ipcc2014kp, p. 2.51]. Australia's inventory instead classed "all fire related GHG emissions (excluding prescribed fires) from that state or territory" as natural once a season passed both tests [@bowman2023wildfire]. The test also depended on the fire record it was run on, since FAOSTAT's series classed `r bc_credits$Year[bc_rule_worst]` as ordinary although British Columbia burned `r format(round(bc_ha(bc_credits$Year[bc_rule_worst])), big.mark = ",")` hectares.

The fire emissions inside both accounts came from one method. Canada's fire matrices assumed high severity throughout, and a severity-based sub-model gave regional emissions typically 10 to 25 per cent lower [@thompson2026incorporating]. Both accounts shared that difference. The account without the disaggregation took nearly all of it, because Canada placed every wildfire on the natural disturbance line [@eccc2026nir].

FAOSTAT's Tier 1 estimate ran a median of `r round(median(gap$Ratio), 1)` times the value Canada submitted. That put the choice of source on the same scale as the choice of method. Part of that gap lay in coefficients the methodological note did not state. FAOSTAT applied the savanna and grassland emission factors to Canada's forest fires, which put its methane at `r round(100 * table_2_5$ch4[1] / table_2_5$ch4[2])` per cent of what its cited method gave. It also placed `r round(100 * sum(savanna_share[["Savanna fires"]]) / sum(savanna_share[["Savanna fires"]] + savanna_share[["Forest fires"]]))` per cent of the area it recorded as burned in savanna, grassland and shrubland items. Those it burned at the fuel values of savanna woodland and grassland and reported without carbon dioxide. Propagated from the spreads of its own tables, the estimate was uncertain by `r round(100 * u_forest[1])` per cent or more, so the check was no more certain than the account it checked. The same database set Canada's organic soil fire emissions to zero while computing them at a mean of `r format(round(mean(obs[["CO2 (kt)"]])), big.mark = ",")` kilotonnes of carbon dioxide a year over the satellite record [@fao2025fires].

The buffers withheld against reversal did not follow the fire regime of the land they covered. ART TREES applied 25 per cent to every country or province unless three mitigating factors were met [@art2021trees]. The Forest Carbon Partnership Facility added 0 to 5 percentage points for exposure to natural disturbance [@fcpf2024buffer]. Only Verra's tool scored the history of events in the area itself, and then for projects rather than countries [@verra2024nprt]. North American conifer forests were among those with the highest reversal risk [@wu2026global]. That risk was grounds for buffer contributions set from regional fire regime statistics. The contributions prepared for the carbon removals regulation of the European Union were set that way, from modelled regional loss to disturbance [@marinelli2026risk].

Crediting standards inherited the silence of the guidance. ART TREES allowed natural disturbance to be excluded on the authority of the guidance without saying how far back the record must reach [@art2025trees3; @ogle2019generic]. Two countries applying the same clause to the same fire record could therefore report different natural shares. The share depended on how far back their labelling reached and how long their regrowth ran. Five changes would close the gap. The first was to specify the record length behind any natural disturbance test. The second was to state the regrowth period over which later removals were disaggregated. The third was to take the uncertainty deduction from gross emissions and gross removals rather than from a net near zero. The fourth was to set buffer contributions from the regional fire regime. The fifth was to exclude only the emissions above a background level, as the Kyoto Protocol provision did. A threshold rule would then not credit the ordinary share of an extreme year's fires.

Two limits qualified these results. The first was that the uncertainty analysis applied one published interval to every annual value and treated each year's error as independent. The shared share bounded the independence assumption without removing it, because the activity data and emission factor uncertainties the standard required were not published for the two lines. The second limit was that all three accounts used Canada's figures as reported. The study therefore compared three sums of one model's output, with fire matrices that assumed high severity [@thompson2026incorporating], and FAOSTAT was its only independent estimate.

# Conclusions

Disaggregating natural disturbance decided whether Canada had a forest carbon credit to claim under ART TREES for 2017 to 2024, and it did not make that credit precise. With the disaggregation, Canada's managed land achieved `r round(sum(credits[["Disaggregated reductions (Mt)"]][split_pos]), 1)` Mt of carbon dioxide equivalent under the standard's crediting level and deductions. Without it the same land fell `r format(abs(credits[["Undisaggregated reductions (Mt)"]][worst]), big.mark = ",")` Mt short in 2023 alone. A country or province in a megafire regime could therefore report a creditable balance only by excluding the fires, under guidance that set no record length for doing so. Under Australia's rule, which excluded natural disturbance only in extreme fire years, the same land achieved `r round(sum(credits[["Australian rule reductions (Mt)"]][rule_pos]), 1)` Mt, `r round(sum(credits[["Australian rule reductions (Mt)"]][rule_pos]) / sum(credits[["Disaggregated reductions (Mt)"]][split_pos]), 1)` times the account Canada reported. The disaggregated account remained uncertain by more than its own size, with uncertainty deductions of `r format(min(uncertainty[["Disaggregated deduction (%)"]], na.rm = TRUE), big.mark = ",")` to `r format(max(uncertainty[["Disaggregated deduction (%)"]], na.rm = TRUE), big.mark = ",")` per cent. It kept part of its reductions only in `r mc_split$Year[which(banked > 0)]`, `r round(banked[which(banked > 0)], 1)` per cent of them. Every positive year kept a credit only if more than `r round(100 * rho_needed, 1)` per cent of the error variance was shared between years, a share the inventory did not report. FAOSTAT's fire estimate for Canada, the independent check a government used, applied savanna emission factors and savanna fuel values that its method did not state. Propagated from its own tables, that estimate was uncertain by `r round(100 * u_forest[1])` per cent or more. Standards that relied on the disaggregation needed a stated record length, a stated regrowth period and the exclusion of only the emissions above a background level. They also needed an uncertainty deduction on gross emissions and removals, and buffers set from regional fire regimes.
